verdict: Lend selectively in Mirzapur carpets — OK overall, but only to exporters and organised loom owners with verified order books; avoid pure job-work units and traders with stretched working capital.
title: Mirzapur Carpets & Rugs: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Mirzapur carpet unit buys wool, cotton or silk yarn, dyes it, and pays hand-knotters to weave a rug over weeks, then sells to a trader or exporter who ships it out.** The cash cycle is the whole credit story: a hand-made carpet takes 30-40 days to make, and traders say quality work can stretch to six months [1]. So when a proposal lands, check the order book and buyer confirmation first; if the unit cannot show a named buyer for the specific piece in production, ask who bears the inventory risk.

That tells you the margin is in the high-end piece, and the working capital is trapped in it for months. So when a proposal lands, check whether the unit sells finished pieces or does job-work for a trader; if it is job-work, ask for the trader's payment record, because the unit carries yarn cost but not pricing power.

## What has changed now
**The local signal is demand-led, not distress-led.** Uttar Pradesh GST collections grew 14.2% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1%, 8.1 pp faster [D], and India-wide carpet-relevant textile output (IIP NIC 13) is up 13.1% YoY [D]. UP electricity demand grew 8.6% Apr-to-date, 0.9 pp slower than India [D] — neutral, no power-cost shock. Peer results are mixed and mostly foreign or national: Oriental Weavers revenue rose 34% y-o-y with 16.6% EBITDA margin [4] (Egypt-listed, EGP), while Faze Three's FY26 revenue rose 32.92% to Rs 932.76 crore but operating profit fell 20.15% to Rs 42.04 crore [5]. **Read that as: volumes are there, margins are not guaranteed.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue organised loom owners with export or metro-retail buyers, and units supplying the festival and heritage-hotel trade [3].** Avoid pure traders with no loom base and units whose entire output goes to one buyer. Structure as a cash-flow loan sized to the production cycle, not a demand loan. Take every month: buyer-wise sales register, yarn purchase bills, and stock statement of work-in-progress pieces. Covenant on working-capital utilisation — a carpet peer ran at around 80% utilisation for twelve months with cash of Rs 0.22 crore [10], and that is the profile to refuse.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the work-in-progress ageing and the buyer concentration.** If a piece sits beyond six months [1], the design has failed in the market — stop further disbursement and inspect stock. If a single buyer crosses half of sales, ask for that buyer's payment history. If yarn inventory is built beyond the order book, ask why — Welspun's 4-5 months of cotton cover [6] is a large mill's hedge, not a small unit's. Rating reports flag inventory management as the key sensitivity [8].
watch: Any piece beyond 6 months -> stop disbursement, inspect stock
Above 80% for 3 months -> freeze enhancement, seek cash flow plan
Single buyer above 50% of sales -> ask for that buyer's payment record
Stock beyond confirmed orders -> ask why, reduce limit
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
